Boiler steam production and associated CO emissions for paper drying 56 2 8 DE-EE0009395 Introduction and Background Conventional drying processes used in the pulp and paper industry primarily involve lengthy, inefficient, multi-cylinder conductive drying with thermal efficiencies ranging from 20-60% and often use fossil-based energy. The current technology involves alternating, one-sided heating of the wet paper web, using steam heated dryer cans wrapped with a dryer fabric. A modern paper machine uses up to 80 of these dryer cans which are 6 feet (ft) in diameter and made of cast iron or steel. Thermal energy is provided in the dryer can by steam condensing on the inside. The overall heat transfer resistance during drying includes resistance through the porous material and resistances from the condensate layer, dryer wall, and corrosion scale.
